unit.title: Utilise sensory skills in beauty service for optimal client experience

summary: This unit teaches you to use sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste to give clients a safe, comfortable and enjoyable beauty service: notice what a client is feeling, communicate clearly and listen well, use touch professionally with consent, manage light, sound, smell and temperature in the salon, adapt for clients with different needs, use your senses to stay safe, and ask for feedback and keep records.

blocks.p: Every client who walks into a salon arrives with her five senses switched on. She sees how clean it is, hears the music and the voices, feels the chair and your hands, smells the products and the towels, and may taste the drink you offer her. Before you have said much, she has already made up her mind about whether she feels welcome and safe. This unit teaches you to use the same five senses to give her a better experience and to keep her safe. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and it supports every other service.

Sensory skills are not tricks. They are the habits of a careful, kind professional: **notice, ask, adjust, check**. You notice that the client is tense, you ask about it, you adjust the pressure or the temperature, and you check that she is better.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's salon: setting up a sensory-friendly station and giving a short relaxing hand or scalp massage, and role plays of the client's visit for clients with different needs. The assessor watches how you greet, listen, explain, ask consent, adapt and check, not only the finished service.

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hair, hands and work area. Never photograph a client's or model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.

sections.title: The five senses and the client experience

blocks.p: The **client experience** is everything the client sees, hears, feels, smells and tastes from the moment she arrives to the moment she leaves. A good experience makes her feel safe, respected and cared for. She comes back, and she tells her family and friends. A poor one costs the salon clients, and can mean accidents and complaints.

head: Sense
What you notice from the client
What the client notices from you and the salon
rows: Sight
Her face and body language: tense, tired, in pain, happy; the state of her skin and hair; reactions such as redness; eyes blinking from spray
A clean, tidy, well-lit salon; a neat, clean you; clear signs; a smile; a mirror she can see herself in
Hearing
What she says and how she says it; sighs, silence; her questions; noises from equipment
Your tone, your words, the music, the dryers and the other conversations
Touch
Whether the hair is dry, rough, oily or tangled; heat or swelling on the skin; tension in her muscles
How you hold her head; the pressure; the temperature of water, tools and towels; a comfortable chair and cape
Smell
Warning smells such as burning hair, gas or fumes; the smell of towels and tools
Fresh air, clean towels, pleasant or fragrance-free products; the smell of chemicals and cigarette smoke
Taste
Whether she can have a drink or snack; allergies and needs
A cool drink or water on a hot day; food kept away from chemicals

ul: A client is more relaxed and trusting when she feels welcome and safe.
Noticing small signs (a wince, a sigh, a closed eye) stops small problems becoming accidents and complaints.
A good experience brings repeat clients and word-of-mouth business, which matters most to a small Jamaican salon.
You protect yourself and the salon: clients who feel listened to are less likely to complain, and your records show what you did.

flow: Notice a sign through one of your senses
Ask the client about it, kindly and simply
Check that she is now comfortable
Note any lasting preference on her record card

blocks.note: Example: you notice the client's shoulders are tight and she is frowning during the shampoo (sight and touch). You ask, 'Is the pressure all right?' She says it is too firm. You use a lighter touch and check again. Next time you see 'light pressure' on her card.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Sight: reading the client and the salon

blocks.p: Most clients do not say when they are uncomfortable. They show it. Learn to read the signs.

head: Sign
It may mean
What you do
rows: Smiling, relaxed shoulders, soft eyes, looking closely and happily at the mirror
She is comfortable and pleased
Carry on; thank her
Frowning, tight jaw, gripping the chair arms, holding her breath
Pain, worry or discomfort
Stop and ask what is wrong; adjust pressure, heat or position
Arms crossed, little eye contact, short answers, sighing
She is unhappy, shy or unsure
Ask an open question and listen
Blinking, rubbing her eyes, turning her face away
Spray, fumes or hair in her eyes
Shield her face; ventilate; stop spraying
Looking at her watch or phone often
She is worried about time
Tell her how long you will take
Pale, sweaty, light-headed, swaying
She may faint or be unwell
Stop; sit or lay her safely; give air; get first-aid help
Redness, swelling or a rash on the skin
A reaction to a product or heat
Stop the service; rinse; tell your instructor

blocks.note: Body language is not always the same in every person. A client who is quiet may simply be tired. Do not guess: **ask**.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Good, bright light at the station lets you see your work clearly and spot problems such as scalp conditions, uneven colour or a reaction.
**Natural daylight** is best for checking the true colour of hair or nail polish. If you must use a lamp, use one that gives daylight-like light.
Soft, warm light in the waiting and relaxing areas helps clients feel calm.
Light should not shine into the client's eyes during treatments.
Look at the finished work from the front, sides and back, in the mirror.
Look for evenness, balance and neatness, and compare both sides.
Show the client the back with a hand mirror and ask whether she is happy.

blocks.h: How you and your salon look

head: Look at
What the client should see
rows: The entrance and waiting area
Clean, tidy, no hair on the floor, no old towels or open products, chairs in good order
Your station
Clear of clutter; tools clean and laid out; mirror clean
You
Clean uniform, tied-back hair, clean hands and short nails, closed shoes, a neat look and a name badge if the salon uses one
The staff
Working, not eating at the stations or shouting across the salon; phones put away
Signs and information
Prices, opening hours and a clear complaints and safety notice

blocks.note: A comb with hair and grease on it, a dirty basin or a pile of damp towels tell a client at once that the salon is not clean or safe, whatever you say.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Hearing is about two things: what you hear and what the client hears from you. Listening well, speaking clearly and keeping the noise at the right level make clients feel respected.

ul: Give the client your **full attention**: face her, put down your phone, and do not talk over her.
Do not interrupt. Let her finish.
Show you are listening with eye contact, a nod and short words ('I see', 'Yes').
Ask **open questions** that start with what, how, when or why ('What would you like to change?'). Closed questions get only 'yes' or 'no'.
Repeat back what you heard to check you understood ('So you want it shorter at the back, and not too much off the top?').
Listen to how she says it, not only the words: tone and pauses tell you a lot.

head: Kind
What it is
Good practice
rows: Verbal
The words and the tone you use
Plain words, a calm, warm tone, a clear voice, the client's name; no slang or jargon she does not know; no shouting
Non-verbal
Your face, eyes, posture, hands and the space between you
Smile; eye contact; open posture; no folded arms, eye-rolling or looking at the clock

ul: A calm, warm tone helps a client relax. A loud, fast or sharp voice makes her tense, however polite the words.
Do not whisper to other staff in front of a client. She may think it is about her.
Be careful with personal topics. Keep to subjects that the client is comfortable with.

blocks.p: **Empathy** is understanding and sharing how another person feels. A nervous first-time client does not need a lecture. She needs to hear 'I understand it can feel strange the first time. I will tell you each step.'

ul: Keep background music **calm and low**, so that clients and staff can talk easily. Choose clean, mild music that suits most clients.
Keep television, phones and staff voices down.
Dryers and clippers are loud: warn the client before you switch them on near her head, and keep them away from clients who are upset by noise.
**Listen for warning sounds**: a rattling dryer motor, a hissing gas pipe, a buzzing or sparking socket, a client's cry or gasp. Act at once: switch off, take the item out of use, and report it.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, your first words are often a warm 'Good morning' or 'Good afternoon' with a smile. Greeting each client, and the person with her, shows respect and sets the tone for the visit.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Stay calm and speak quietly, in private if you can
Show empathy and thank her for telling you
Repeat back the problem to agree it
Offer a fair solution within your authority, or call your supervisor
Record what happened and what you agreed

ul: Never argue, blame the client or make excuses. A client who is listened to and treated fairly often stays loyal.
If you cannot decide, say so and call the supervisor. Do not promise what you cannot give.

sections.title: Touch: professional, safe and with consent

blocks.p: Touch is the sense you use most in a beauty service, and the one that most easily crosses a line. The rule is simple: **explain first, get consent, touch only where needed, and stop if the client asks**.

ul: **Explain what you will do** before you touch her: 'I am going to wash your hair now. I will support your head.' Ask whether that is all right.
Never touch a client suddenly from behind. Say what you are doing and let her see you.
Use clean, warm, dry hands with short nails. Wash your hands before you start.
Use a calm, firm, smooth touch. Hesitant, light touch can tickle; sharp, quick touch frightens.
Touch **only the areas needed** for the service. Do not hug or touch a client without being asked.
Respect her preferences. Some clients dislike being touched on the head or face, or have religious or cultural reasons.
Avoid broken, bruised, sunburned or infected skin. Do not massage over cuts, sores or swellings.
Stop at once if she asks, or if she shows pain or alarm.

blocks.note: **Consent** means the client agrees to be touched or treated, after you have explained what will happen. Consent can be taken back at any time. Silence is not consent: ask.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Pressure**: how hard or softly your hands press. Start light, ask 'Is the pressure all right?', and watch her face. Never use the same pressure on everyone, and never press as hard as you can.
**Temperature**: test water, steam, wax, oils, towels and hot tools before they touch the client. Test water on the inside of your wrist, then ask her.
Warm, not hot, towels and cool, not icy, hands help comfort.

head: Movement
How you do it
Effect
rows: Effleurage
Light, slow, smooth stroking with the palms or the flats of the fingers
Relaxing; used to start and end a massage and to spread product
Petrissage
Slow, firm kneading: press, lift and release the skin or scalp
Eases tension; improves circulation
Friction
Small, brisk circles or rubbing with the finger pads
Stimulating; helps loosen the skin or scalp
Tapotement (percussion)
Light, quick tapping with the fingertips
Stimulating; used briefly and lightly

ul: Always use the **pads of the fingers**, never the nails.
Check for contra-indications first: cuts, sores, infections, sunburn, recent injury, swelling, or a client who says it hurts.
A hand or scalp massage should be slow and rhythmic, with no sudden jumps in pressure.
Keep your own posture good: stand with a straight back, so you do not tire and press unevenly.

head: What you feel
What it may mean
rows: Hair that feels dry, rough, gummy or oily
Its condition and what treatment it needs
A scalp that feels hot, swollen or tender
A reaction or infection; stop and ask
Tight shoulders and a stiff neck
Tension or discomfort; adjust the position and the pressure
Water or a tool that feels too hot
Adjust it at once

blocks.note: Wear gloves when the service needs them, but your hands still tell you a lot. Notice heat on the scalp, swelling, or bumps, and ask about stinging during chemical services.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Smell is the sense that is most linked to memory and mood. A fresh, clean salon feels cared for. A salon that smells of stale towels, damp mildew, cigarette smoke or strong chemicals feels unclean.

head: Source
What to do
rows: Chemical products (relaxer, colour, perm, nail products)
Work in a well-ventilated room; keep lids on; keep fumes away from other clients
Towels, gowns and capes
Launder them in hot water with detergent and dry them completely; damp towels grow bacteria and smell; keep clean ones in a closed cupboard
Bins and drains
Empty and clean them often
Perfume and scented products
Keep scents light. Offer fragrance-free choices. Never cover chemical smells with extra perfume or air fresheners
You
Be clean, wear fresh clothes, and avoid strong perfume or smoke

blocks.p: Your nose can warn you of danger. Act quickly and correctly.

head: Smell
May mean
What you do
rows: Burning hair or skin
A tool is too hot, or hair or skin is being burnt
Lift the tool away; check the hair and skin; lower the heat
Burning plastic or hot electrics
A faulty dryer or socket
Switch off and unplug; take it out of use; report it
Gas
A leak
No flames and no switches; open windows; get everyone out; report it
Strong fumes from products
Poor ventilation or a spill
Open windows; close lids; clean the spill; help any client who feels unwell
A musty smell on towels, braids or locs
Damp and mildew
Wash and dry fully; advise the client

ul: Some clients get headaches, sneezing or asthma from strong scents. Ask about this at the consultation and note it on the record card.

**Essential oils** are strong plant oils. They can irritate the skin, cause allergy, upset breathing and, for some oils, are not suitable in pregnancy or for some conditions. They are never swallowed.
Use them only as the maker's instructions say: usually **diluted in a carrier oil** and never put neat on the skin.
Ask about allergies, asthma, pregnancy and skin conditions first. Do a skin test where the maker says. Avoid the eyes and broken skin.
Stop at once if a client reacts, and store oils closed and out of the sun and out of children's reach.
Offer a **fragrance-free** choice for sensitive clients.

blocks.p: A cool drink on a hot Jamaican day is part of a good service. Offering it well means doing it safely.

ul: **Ask about allergies and needs** first (nuts, diabetes, religious reasons, pregnancy).
Serve water or a drink in a clean cup or glass, in the waiting area or at a safe station, not near chemicals or at the basin.
Keep food and drink **away from chemicals**: never store them on the trolley or in the same fridge as products.
Clean spills at once. Wash and dry cups and glasses after each use.
Do not eat at the station in front of clients.

blocks.note: A client who is diabetic or pregnant may need a snack on time during a long service, such as braiding. Ask at the consultation, and agree breaks.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The atmosphere of the salon and the client's visit

blocks.p: **Ambience** is the overall feeling of the salon, made by its lighting, sound, smell, temperature, cleanliness and decor. You may not own the salon, but you help make its atmosphere every day.

head: Element
Good practice
Poor practice
rows: Cleanliness
Floors swept after each client; stations wiped; used towels in a covered bin; clean basins; bins emptied
Hair on the floor; towels piled on chairs; dirty combs
Light
Bright at stations; softer in the waiting area; daylight where possible
Dim, flickering or glaring lights; light in the client's eyes
Sound
Calm music at a low volume; staff voices kept down; dryers off when not in use
Loud music; phones ringing; shouting across the salon; rude lyrics
Temperature and air
Comfortably cool with a fan or air conditioning; fresh air; a light cover offered
Hot and stuffy; icy air conditioning with no cover; fumes
Smell
Fresh, ventilated, light or no scent
Strong chemicals, stale towels, smoke, heavy perfume
Seating and space
Comfortable chairs; neck rests; clear walkways; reading material in the waiting area
Clutter; broken chairs; cables across the floor
Welcome
A smile, a greeting by name, an offer of a seat and a drink
Ignoring the client; staff eating or chatting

blocks.h: The client's journey: using the senses at each step

head: Step
What you do
rows: Arrival and greeting
Smile, say hello, use her name, offer a seat. Notice her mood and how she walks in.
Waiting
Tell her how long. Offer a drink and something to read. Keep the area clean and calm.
Consultation
Good light; sit or stand at her level; ask open questions; listen actively; note her preferences, allergies and needs.
The service
Explain each step; ask consent; check pressure and temperature; keep noise down; check comfort often; offer breaks on long services.
Checking the result
Use good light and the mirror; show the back; ask whether she is happy.
Feedback and payment
Ask for feedback and listen; thank her; give aftercare advice; take payment politely.
Departure and records
Offer to rebook; say goodbye warmly; write her preferences on the record card.

blocks.note: Being **on time** (punctuality) is part of a good experience. If you are running late, tell the client, apologise and give a new time. Do not leave her waiting without a word.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In Jamaica's heat, a client who has come in from the sun or walked far will feel better with a cool drink, a fan and a few minutes to settle before the service.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Every client is different. Some need extra patience, a different way of communicating, or a change in the room. The principles are the same: **ask, do not assume; treat her with respect; give her choice and control**.

head: Client
How to help
rows: Blind or partly sighted
Introduce yourself and say who else is there
Offer your arm, never push or grab her
Describe where the chair and basin are, and each step before you touch her
Keep walkways clear; tell her where her bag and belongings are
Describe the finished result and read out product names or prices if she asks
Deaf or hard of hearing
Face her, in good light, and speak clearly and at a normal pace, without shouting
Reduce background noise
Use notes, gestures or a phone text; use Jamaican Sign Language if you or a helper know it
Agree a signal for 'stop' or 'too hot'
Check that she has understood; do not turn your back while talking
Sensitive to light, noise or scent (for example, after migraines or with autism or anxiety)
Offer a quieter seat, softer light and calm explanations
Use fragrance-free products where possible
Warn her before a dryer or clipper starts
Offer breaks
Wheelchair user or limited movement
Ask how she prefers to transfer; keep the way clear; use a front-wash basin or a basin she can reach
Do not move her chair without asking
Older client
Allow more time; offer a hand getting in and out of the chair
Be gentle with the neck at the basin and ask about dizziness
Make sure she is warm enough
Nervous or first-time client, or someone who has had a bad experience
Explain each step before you do it
Go slowly; check often
Let her say 'stop'
Reassure her calmly
A child
Speak kindly at her level; explain simply
Ask the parent about allergies; keep the touch light; take breaks
Never leave a child alone in the chair
A client from a different culture or faith
Ask how she likes her hair or skin handled and what products she accepts
Respect her wishes and her privacy
Do not make assumptions

ul: Treat every client fairly, whatever her race, religion, age, disability or background. This is a matter of respect and, in Jamaica, of law that protects persons with disabilities from discrimination.
Speak to the client herself, not only to the person with her.
Use respectful words, and ask how she would like to be addressed.
Keep her information private.

blocks.note: Jamaican Sign Language (JSL) is the sign language used by many deaf people in Jamaica. If a deaf client brings an interpreter or a family member, speak to the client, not the interpreter.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Staying safe through your senses; feedback and records

blocks.h: Using your senses to keep everyone safe

head: Sense
Warning you may notice
Action
rows: Sight
A client who goes pale or swollen; redness on the skin; a spill on the floor; a damaged plug or cable; hair on the floor
Stop; help the client; wipe up; take damaged items out of use; sweep
Hearing
A rattling dryer; a hissing gas pipe; a client saying it stings or burns; a cry or gasp
Switch off; take out of use; stop the service; rinse if it is a chemical; report
Touch
Heat or swelling on the scalp; water or a tool too hot; a hot dryer casing
Rinse or stop; adjust; test water on the inside of your wrist; cool the tool
Smell
Burning hair, gas, strong fumes, burning plastic
Lift the tool; evacuate; ventilate; report
Taste
A client with a food allergy; a drink near chemicals
Ask first; keep food and drink away from products

blocks.note: If the client says her scalp is burning during a chemical service, **rinse the product off at once** with plenty of lukewarm water and tell your instructor. Never tell her to wait until the timer ends. If a client faints or looks very unwell, stop the service, make her safe, and call first aid.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Read the label and the safety data sheet (the maker's sheet that gives hazards and first aid) before using a product.
Keep your work area clean, tidy and well lit. Clear clutter and cables.
Know where the first aid kit, the eyewash and the exits are.
Ask every client at the end of the service: 'Are you happy with how it looks and how it felt?'
Ask about comfort, such as the water temperature and the pressure. Listen without defending.
Say 'Thank you for telling me; I will check that more carefully' and mean it. Never reply 'That is not my job' or 'That is how everyone likes it'.
Pass serious comments to your supervisor, and use small ones to improve.

blocks.p: Write the client's preferences on her **record card** so that the next visit is just as comfortable, whoever serves her.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, name, contact details
07/11/2026, Yvonne Campbell, Mandeville
Preferences
Prefers lighter pressure; likes warm, not hot, water; likes quiet music
Allergies and sensitivities
Headaches from strong scents; use fragrance-free products
Needs
Partly sighted: describe each step; keep walkways clear
Feedback
Very happy; asked for a quieter chair next time
Problems
Complained about hot water; adjusted; no further problem
Stylist
J. Taylor (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Client records are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure: store cards in a locked drawer or a password-protected system, and never discuss a client's needs, health or complaints with other clients.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can name the five senses and say how each affects the client's experience.
I can use 'notice, ask, adjust, check' in a service.
I can read a client's body language and facial expression.
I can use light well, including daylight to check colour.
I can keep my station, my appearance and the salon looking clean and tidy.
I can listen actively, ask open questions and repeat back what I heard.
I can use a calm, warm tone and show empathy.
I can keep music and noise at the right level and notice warning sounds.
I can handle an unhappy client calmly, offer a fair solution and record it.
I can use touch professionally: explain, get consent, touch only where needed and stop when asked.
I can check pressure and temperature, and use effleurage, petrissage, friction and tapotement correctly.
I can keep the air fresh, offer fragrance-free choices and use essential oils safely.
I can respond correctly to burning, gas and fume smells.
I can offer refreshments safely after an allergy check.
I can describe the atmosphere of a good salon and the client's journey from arrival to departure.
I can adapt for clients who are blind, deaf, sensitive to light, noise or scent, older, nervous or from different cultures.
I can use my senses to keep clients and staff safe.
I can ask for feedback, accept it kindly and write preferences on a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give an example for each point. For example: 'Touch: I test the water on the inside of my wrist and then ask the client, so that it does not scald her.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Everything the client sees, hears, feels, smells and tastes during her visit.
Using the five senses to give a better, safer service.
The messages we give with our face, hands and posture instead of words.
Communication without words: eye contact, smile, posture and gestures.
Communication with words and tone of voice.
Giving full attention and checking that you have understood.
A question that starts with what, how, when or why and needs more than yes or no.
Understanding and sharing how another person feels.
A client's agreement to be touched or treated, after you have explained.
How hard or softly your hands press.
Light, slow stroking used to relax and to spread product.
Brisk rubbing in small circles with the finger pads.
Light, quick tapping with the fingertips.
The overall feeling of a salon, made by its light, sound, smell, temperature and cleanliness.
Fresh air moving through the room to carry fumes away.
A strong plant oil that must be diluted and used with care.
A mild oil used to dilute essential oils.
The maker's sheet giving a product's hazards and first-aid steps.
The sign language used by many deaf people in Jamaica.
Treating every client fairly, whatever her race, religion, age or disability.
The client's comments on how the service went.
The client's record of her details, preferences, needs, services and feedback.

c1.title: A partly sighted client in Kingston
c1.text: Mrs. Lorna Spence, 70, comes to a salon in Kingston for a wash and set. She is partly sighted and walks with a white cane. She arrives on the arm of her daughter, who then goes to park the car. Trainee Orlando greets her at the door. The walkway has a cable from a dryer across it, and the chair at his station is in a different place from last time.

c2.title: A deaf client in Montego Bay
c2.text: Racquel Sinclair, 24, is deaf and communicates in Jamaican Sign Language and by writing, and can lip-read a little. She comes alone to a busy salon in Montego Bay for a wash and trim. Music is loud and three dryers are running. Trainee Janelle does not know sign language, starts to talk quickly while turning to pick up a towel, and then asks 'Do you understand?' while looking at the floor.

c3.title: A client who reacts to scent and light in Mandeville
c3.text: Mrs. Paulette Dixon, 52, tells trainee Garth that she has migraines triggered by strong smells and bright light, and that loud noise upsets her. The salon in Mandeville has a scented candle burning at the front desk, bright lights above every station, and a dryer running close to her chair. Garth wants to use a heavily scented oil during her scalp massage.

c4.title: A nervous first-time client in Spanish Town
c4.text: Sasha Williams, 19, comes to a salon in Spanish Town for her first professional shampoo and scalp massage. She says that a stylist once pulled her hair hard and scratched her scalp, and she is nervous. During the shampoo, trainee Roy notices she is gripping the chair arms and holding her breath. He is using firm friction movements and has not told her what he is going to do next.

c5.title: Running late and a complaint in Portmore
c5.text: At a salon in Portmore, Miss Cheryl Reid has waited 40 minutes for her 10:00 a.m. appointment without being told why. The waiting area has damp towels on the chairs and no one has greeted her. When trainee Dwight finally starts her trim, she says it is shorter than she asked. She looks upset and crosses her arms.

questions.q: What should Orlando do first when Mrs. Spence arrives at the door?
o: Take her arm firmly and guide her to the chair
Greet her, say who he is, and offer his arm
Wait inside until she finds the way herself
Speak loudly so that she can hear where he is
questions.why: Introduce yourself and say who you are, then offer your arm and let her take it. Never grab or push a partly sighted client, and do not shout: she does not need it.

questions.q: What should be done about the cable across the walkway?
o: Leave it, because Mrs. Spence has a cane to feel with
Warn her about the cable as she walks past it
Tape the cable down and carry on with the shampoo
Move it so the walkway is clear before she comes through
questions.why: A clear walkway is the first safety step for any visually impaired client. A cane does not always show a cable in time, and a warning leaves the danger in place.

questions.q: How should Orlando prepare Mrs. Spence for the shampoo?
o: Describe where the chair and basin are, then each step first
Move her quickly to the basin so that she does not wait
Tell her the steps only after he has started the shampoo
Tell her daughter, and let the daughter explain it to her
questions.why: A client who cannot see needs words in place of sight. Describe the layout and each step before you act, and speak to the client herself, not to the person with her.

questions.q: How can Orlando help Mrs. Spence at the end of the service?
o: Hand her a mirror, since the result is something for her to see
Say only 'All done' and take her through to the till
Describe the style, and tell her where her bag and cane are
Ask her daughter whether the style looks acceptable
questions.why: A client with low vision gets the same chance to check the result when you describe it. Telling her where her belongings are keeps her safe and in control.

questions.q: What is the main problem with Janelle's way of speaking to Racquel?
o: She is speaking too slowly for a client to follow
She faces away while talking, so Racquel cannot see her
She is using a language that Racquel has never learnt
She is asking too many questions in the first minute
questions.why: A client who lip-reads or uses signs must see your face and hands. Face her, in good light, and speak clearly and at a normal pace; do not talk while turned away.

questions.q: Which change would best help Racquel communicate?
o: Turn up the music, so the whole salon feels livelier
Use notes or gestures, lower the noise and agree a 'stop' signal
Speak loudly so that Racquel can feel the sound of her voice
Ask another client in the salon to talk to her instead
questions.why: Notes, gestures, less background noise and an agreed signal all give a deaf client control. Shouting does not help, and asking another client breaks her privacy.

questions.q: Racquel says through a note that she would like the water cooler. How should Janelle respond?
o: Nod and carry on, since the water is already warm enough
Test the water on her wrist, adjust it and check with her by sight
Ask a colleague to decide what temperature is best for her
Tell her the water has to be warm for the shampoo to clean
questions.why: Acting on a deaf client's request, testing the water and checking again by sight shows respect and keeps her safe. The client's comfort decides the water temperature.

questions.q: Which change would help Mrs. Dixon most?
o: Offer a quieter chair, softer light and no scent
Give her a stronger scent to cover the smell of the candle
Ask her to put on sunglasses and earphones while she is served
Keep the candle and bright lights, but work more quickly
questions.why: She has told you what triggers her migraines. A quieter seat, softer light and fragrance-free surroundings remove the triggers. Covering one smell with another, or asking her to cope, does not.

questions.q: Garth wants to use a heavily scented oil. What should he do?
o: Use it, but dilute it with some water first
Use it, but only half the amount he planned to use
Use it, because the oil is meant to help her relax
Use a fragrance-free product, after asking her
questions.why: A client who reacts to strong scents should be offered fragrance-free products. Essential oils are strong, and diluting or reducing them does not make them safe for a scent-triggered migraine.

questions.q: Which warning should Garth give before he turns on the dryer near Mrs. Dixon?
o: Say nothing, so as not to alarm her
Tell her to cover her ears when it starts
Warn her it is about to start and offer to move her
Ask her to leave the chair until he has finished drying
questions.why: Warning the client lets her prepare, and offering to move gives her control. Never surprise a client who is sensitive to sound.

questions.q: Where should Garth note Mrs. Dixon's triggers?
o: Nowhere, because he will remember them himself
On her record card, for any stylist who serves her
On a sticky note on her station mirror
On the salon's noticeboard for all staff to see
questions.why: A record card keeps her needs and preferences private and available to whoever serves her next. A note on a mirror or a noticeboard breaks her privacy.

questions.q: What signs show Roy that Sasha is not comfortable?
o: She is quiet and has her eyes closed
She is gripping the chair arms and holding her breath
She is breathing steadily and her shoulders are low
She smiles when he starts the shampoo
questions.why: Gripping, holding her breath, tight shoulders or a frown are signs of discomfort or fear. A relaxed face and steady breathing show comfort.

questions.q: What should Roy do now?
o: Stop, tell her what comes next and ask about the pressure
Carry on, but press harder so that it feels firm and secure
Tell her firmly to relax and carry on with the shampoo
Carry on in silence until she says something to him
questions.why: Notice, ask, adjust, check. Stopping to explain and ask gives her control. A nervous client with a bad history needs reassurance and a lighter, predictable touch.

questions.q: Which massage movement suits Sasha best at the start of her scalp massage?
o: Quick, brisk friction
Light, quick tapotement
Firm petrissage
Slow, light effleurage
questions.why: Effleurage is a light, slow, smooth stroke that relaxes and reassures. Friction and tapotement are stimulating, and firm kneading can feel threatening to a nervous client.

questions.q: What should Dwight have done about Miss Reid's 40-minute wait?
o: Said nothing, because busy salons often run late
Told her only after her trim had already started
Greeted her, said how long and apologised
Asked her to come back on another day instead
questions.why: Punctuality and communication are part of a good experience. If you are late, say so, apologise, give a new time and make her comfortable.

questions.q: Miss Reid says her trim is shorter than she asked. What is the best first response?
o: Tell her it will grow back, so there is nothing to worry about
Stay calm, listen without interrupting and show empathy
Point out that she was shown the length in the mirror
Call a colleague to explain what she should have asked for
questions.why: Calm listening and empathy come first. Arguing, making excuses or blaming the client makes it worse. Then agree the problem, offer a fair solution or call the supervisor.

questions.q: After the complaint is settled, what should Dwight do?
o: Forget it, since the matter is now over
Tell other clients what happened, so that they know
Remove her card, so that no one sees what happened
Record what happened and was agreed, and learn from it
questions.why: A record of the complaint and the agreed solution helps the salon improve and protects you. Do not discuss it with other clients.

questions.q: A client asks for a cold drink halfway through a long service. What should you do first?
o: Give her the drink at once, on the trolley at the basin
Ask about allergies and needs, then serve it away from products
Refuse, because drinks are never allowed in a salon
Ask her to leave the chair and fetch it herself
questions.why: Ask about allergies and needs before serving food or drink, and keep it well away from chemicals. A cool drink during a long service is part of a good experience.

questions.q: Why should you check the pressure with a client during a scalp massage?
o: Because pressure wears out your fingers over time
Because the right pressure differs between clients, and she may not say
Because firm pressure is required by every salon's rules
Because all clients like the lightest touch possible
questions.why: People differ, and many will not complain. Ask and watch her face, then adjust. Never use the same pressure on every client, or the hardest you can.

questions.q: The salon's towels smell stale and damp. What is the most likely cause?
o: They were not washed hot enough or dried fully
They were washed too often and the fabric wore thin
They were washed with too much detergent
They were folded before they had cooled down
questions.why: Towels washed too cool, or not dried completely, grow bacteria and mildew and smell. Wash in hot water with detergent, dry fully, and keep clean ones in a closed cupboard.
